paragraphs.heading: Where they are
paragraphs.text: The Appalachian Mountains are a vast range in eastern North America. They stretch from central Alabama to Newfoundland, roughly 2,050 miles (3,300 km), running generally southwest to northeast. The highest peak is Mount Mitchell in North Carolina, at 6,684 feet (2,037 m). The range also takes in Saint Pierre and Miquelon, which is an overseas collectivity of France, so technically it spans parts of three countries.

paragraphs.heading: A very old range
paragraphs.text: The geologic processes that led to the Appalachians began with the creation of the supercontinent Rodinia, around 1.1 billion years ago. Many Precambrian rocks and minerals made in that process can still be seen in the range's outcrops. A series of three distinct orogenies, starting about 480 million years ago, created the modern Appalachians. That makes them among the oldest mountain ranges in the world that still survive.

paragraphs.heading: Worn down over time
paragraphs.text: The young Appalachians reached heights similar to those of the Alps and Rockies today. Both of those are significantly younger ranges. Then came 240 million years of erosion by water, wind, ice and gravity. This gradually turned them into the lower, rugged peaks usually seen today.

paragraphs.heading: Relatives in other ranges
paragraphs.text: The Appalachians are geologically related to the Scottish Highlands, the Atlas Mountains, the Scandinavian Mountains and the Ouachitas. All of these ranges once belonged to the sprawling Central Pangean Mountains. Plate tectonics later tore them apart.

paragraphs.heading: Forests and climate
paragraphs.text: Given their great length, the Appalachians hold a wide mix of biomes, from temperate broadleaf and mixed forest in the south to boreal forest in the north. In the north and at high elevations, conifers such as red spruce and balsam fir dominate. Deciduous trees such as sugar maple and beech are more common further south, with oak-chestnut forests in between. The climate runs from humid subtropical to subarctic. A few peaks of the Presidential Range, in New Hampshire's White Mountains, have a true tundra climate.

paragraphs.heading: A barrier to travel
paragraphs.text: The Appalachians are a barrier to east–west travel. They form a series of alternating ridgelines and valleys that lie across the direction of most highways and railroads running east–west. In the colonial era this barrier did a great deal to shape how the United States expanded.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: In 1528 members of the Narváez expedition, exploring inland along the northern coast of Florida, came upon a Native American village near present-day Tallahassee. They wrote its name down as Apalchen or Apalachen. The Spanish soon changed the name to Apalachee and used it for the tribe and the region. After Hernando de Soto's expedition of 1540, Spanish mapmakers began to apply the tribe's name to the mountains themselves. It was not commonly used for the whole range until the late 19th century.
